messages.subject: AW: posterior samples - negative binomial model
messages.subject_clean: AW: posterior samples - negative binomial model
messages.body_plain:
Dear Sonia

What your colleagues suggested is called a posterior predictive check for goodness of fit (see Gelman et al. 1996 and Conn et al., Ecol. Mono, 2018). It’s based on the following sensible idea: if a model fits your data, then when you simulate new data under that model (using the values of parameters as estimated from your data), then these data should resemble your actual data.

So you have to add in your code one or more lines that produce samples from the predictive distribution of the data. The simplest way to do this would be to add the red bit in your first block of code below. When you monitor  captures.new <http://captures.new>, you will get one sampled value of each datum i at every iteration of the MCMC algorithm.

Note that there is a twist here for hierarchical models like yours, where you may simulate new data either based on the estimated random effects or else you may also resample new values for the random effects (the alpha’s in your case). I don’t go into this but refer you to the vignette “DHARMa for Bayesians” in the R package DHARMa (Hartig, see below).

There are multiple ways in which you can make a comparison between the actual data and the data that would be expected under the model under the assumption that the model fits your actual data (i.e., captures.new <http://captures.new>). One is to calculate some omnibus test statistic such as chisquared or Freeman-Tukey, which are based on the expected values of your response and thus are a function of model residuals.

One pretty widely used R package for goodness of fit assessment in traditional mixed models is DHARMa. There is a vignette that explains how you can use it with existing Bayesian simulations produced by software such as JAGS. Perhaps I’d simply suggest to you to use that.

Best regards  --- Marc

Von: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com> Im Auftrag von Sonia Cebrián Camisón
Gesendet: Donnerstag, 24. August 2023 18:55
An: hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com>
Betreff: posterior samples - negative binomial model

Dear all,

I am working on modeling the effects of climate and landscape on mosquito abundance. Right now, I am working on a model to explore how the wind speed affects the trap effectiveness, with the idea of incorporating this effect into the final model.

I am using jagsUI, and mostly following examples in the AHM books and adapting them to my case study. However, I have little expertise in Bayesian statistics and I am finding some problems in carrying on model checking.

My most basic model right now looks like this:

model{
#likelihood
for (i in 1:N){
  captures[i] ~ dnegbin(p[i], r)
  p[i] <- r/(r+lambda[i])
  log(lambda[i]) <-  alpha[week_num[i]] + beta1*wind2[i]

}
#random effect
for(j in 1:M){
  alpha[j] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha, tau.alpha) # Mean and precision = 1/variance
}

#priors
beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
mu.alpha~dnorm(0, 0.001)
tau.alpha ~ dgamma(1.0E-3, 1.0E-3)
sigma.alpha <- sqrt(1/tau.alpha)
r ~ dunif(0,50)
}

Some colleagues recommended sampling from the posterior distribution of the model’s parameter and developing simulated data to visually compare is they are similar to the observed data or not, as a part of model checking and fit assessment. For this, I thought of doing something similar to AHM Book1 5.9:

# Likelihood of the model
for (i in 1:M){
Cmax[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i]) # note no variance parameter
log(lambda[i]) <- alpha[facFor[i]] + beta[facFor[i]] * elev[i]
resi[i] <- (Cmax[i]-lambda[i]) / (sqrt(lambda[i])+e) # Pearson residual
}

#simulated data

lambda2 <- array(dim = c(15000, 267))
for(j in 1:267){ # Loop over sites
lambda2[,j] <- exp(out5$sims.list$alpha[,facFor[j]] +
out5$sims.list$beta[,facFor[j]] * elev[j]) # linear regression/backtransform
}

However, I do not understand if this would be correct for a negative binomial distribution.

I also noticed that for some fit assessment approaches it is necessary to add a simulated data set like captures.new <http://captures.new>[i] ~ dnegbin(p[I], r) on the model itself. In this case, are we doing the same as in the previous example?

I also thought about using a test statistic to complement the GoF assessment, but I am not sure how I should choose between different options. For example, I have found mixed opinions on whether the Chi-square test statistic would be appropriate or not for a negative binomial distribution.

My apologies if this post results are too beginner-level for this group, but I have been struggling for some time with the model assessment. I would appreciate it if anyone could give me some advice regarding this issue or recommend any bibliography, website or post on the subject.

Cheers,

Sonia.

--
*** Three hierarchical modeling email lists ***
(1) unmarked: for questions specific to the R package unmarked
(2) SCR: for design and Bayesian or non-bayesian analysis of spatial capture-recapture
(3) HMecology (this list): for everything else, especially material covered in the books by Royle & Dorazio (2008), Kéry & Schaub (2012), Kéry & Royle (2016, 2021) and Schaub & Kéry (2022)

messages.subject: Node inconsistent with parents
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I'm very beginner in Jags, this is why I could figure out how to solve the  "Node inconsistent with parents" error message.

I used the following code, but it gives node incosistent error message

Error in checkForRemoteErrors(val) :
  one node produced an error: Error in node n[2]
Node inconsistent with parents
#####################
# JAGS model

library(spatstat)

# Camera data

obs<- read.csv("foxdet_march2014.csv",header=T)
obs<- as.matrix(obs)
colnames(obs)<- 1:dim(obs)[2]
fox.obs<- obs

n<- rowSums(fox.obs,na.rm=T)
K<- apply(fox.obs,1,function(x) length(x[!is.na <http://is.na>(x)]))

# camera locations
locs<- read.csv("camlocs_march2014.csv",header=T)
locs<- locs/1000

xlim<- range(locs[,1])
ylim<- range(locs[,2])
buffer<- 2
xlim[1]<- xlim[1] - buffer
xlim[2]<- xlim[2] + buffer
ylim[1]<- ylim[1] - buffer
ylim[2]<- ylim[2] + buffer
area<- (xlim[2]-xlim[1]) * (ylim[2]-ylim[1])

X<- as.matrix(locs)
M=200
J<- nrow(locs)

data<- list("n","X","M","J","K","xlim","ylim")

inits<- function(){list(sigma=runif(1,0.2,1),g0=runif(1,0.1,0.5),psi=0.5,w=rbinom(200,1,0.5))}

params<- c("N","g0","sigma")

modelFilename = "SPA_JAGS.txt"

cat("
model {

for(i in 1:M) {
  w[i] ~ dbern(psi)
  S[i,1] ~ dunif(xlim[1],xlim[2])
  S[i,2] ~ dunif(ylim[1],ylim[2])

  for(j in 1:J) {
    d2[i,j]<- (S[i,1] - X[j,1])^2 + (S[i,2] - X[j,2])^2
    prob[i,j]<- g0 * exp(-d2[i,j]/2/sigma^2) * w[i]

  }
}

for(j in 1:J) {
  Ptrap[j]<- 1-prod(1-prob[,j])
  n[j] ~ dbin(Ptrap[j],K[j])
  }

sigma ~ dgamma(18,30)
g0 ~ dbeta(1,1)
psi ~ dbeta(1,1)
N<- sum(w)

}
", fill=TRUE, file=modelFilename)

# NOTE increase n.iter in the following to achive convergence if needed.
library(R2jags)
fit.gp <http://fit.gp> = jags.parallel(data=data, inits=inits, params, model.file=modelFilename, n.chains=3, n.iter=2000, n.burnin=1000, n.thin=1)

I appreciate your help

Alaa

messages.subject: Deadline extended: One-year postdoc (modeling wildlife survey data) at the Leibniz-IZW Berlin (earliest start: Nov 1, 2023)
messages.subject_clean: Deadline extended: One-year postdoc (modeling wildlife survey data) at the Leibniz-IZW Berlin (earliest start: Nov 1, 2023)
messages.body_plain:
We - the team Biodiversity Dynamics in the Department of Ecological Dynamics at the Leibniz Institute for Zoo and Wildlife Research in Berlin (ecodynizw.github.io/team-biodiversity.html <https://ecodynizw.github.io/team-biodiversity.html>) - are looking for a post-doc (90 - 100%), starting as soon as November 1, 2023, until October 31st, 2024.

This position will focus on the development and application of modern approaches to process and analyze wildlife survey data. One component of the work will be to analyze camera-trapping and SMART patrol data using a (community) occupancy framework. Further work includes the co-development of an R Shiny App to make the analytical approaches available to a broader scientific and conservation community, and the co-development of AI (convolutional neural network) approaches to locate and classify animals in camera-trap images. This project represents a pilot phase with good chances of receiving additional funding; the postdoc will be involved in developing a proposal for continuation of the project.

We will accept applications until the position is filled.

For more information on the position and how to apply, please visit: https://leibniz-institutfuerzoo-undwildtierforschung.softgarden.io/job/34929244?l=de

Please forward this email to students and colleagues who might be interested.

messages.body_plain:
From: bounce-4870...@mm.list.cornell.edu <bounce-4870...@mm.list.cornell.edu> on behalf of Philipp Boersch-Supan <philipp.bo...@bto.org>
Sent: Thursday, September 21, 2023 10:45
To: euri...@cornell.edu <euri...@cornell.edu>
Subject: Vacancy: Ecological Statistician / Quantitative Ecologist

Dear all,

We are hiring an Ecological Statistician / Quantitative Ecologist (full time, permanent) at the British Trust for Ornithology. Details below.

Thanks for sharing,
Philipp

The British Trust for Ornithology is seeking an Ecological Statistician or Quantitative Ecologist to contribute directly to the design and analysis of a broad range of applied projects and to provide statistical advice and training across the organisation. They will support the Senior Ecological Statistician working on topics such as biodiversity surveys, analyses of large-scale and long-term datasets, analyses of survival and productivity data and the design and analysis of experiments. In addition, the post holder will be required to lead on data analyses and provide statistical input to a wide range of projects, initially including, but not limited to, analytical work for the BTO’s Wetland and Marine Research Team.

The successful applicant will have a quantitative background with a postgraduate degree in a discipline such as Data Science, Statistics, Ecology, or Epidemiology or equivalent professional experience and an interest in ecology or nature conservation. The role requires strong analytical and project management skills, being prepared to be adaptable and getting involved in a wide range of scientific projects, and gaining new skills and knowledge on the job where necessary. Applicants should enjoy, and be effective at, communicating with a wide range of colleagues and stakeholders to understand their evidence needs and provide specific expertise.

This is a permanent, full-time role based at our HQ in Thetford, Norfolk, UK, although you will be able to work from home or from the David Attenborough Building in Cambridge part of the time on a hybrid working regime.

Location: Thetford/Cambridge, United Kingdom
Earnings: £33186.00 + 11% Pension contribution
Contract: Full time, Permanent

Full job description and application form are at  https://britishtrustforornithology.postingpanda.uk/job/461215

Closing date for receipt of applications is 23:59 on Sunday 8th October 2023 and Interviews will be held in Thetford in the week commencing 23 October 2023. UK Right to work is required.

If you have any questions, please contact  recru...@bto.org. For informal enquiries about the role please contact  philipp.bo...@bto.org.
--

messages.subject: data integration - anyone done this?
messages.body_plain: Hi all. We are working on a data integration paper that combines professionally collected data with community science data to inform a Dail-Madsen style model (i.e., estimates population vital rates). Like everyone else, we want to claim our work is novel without necessarily implementing a rigorous and comprehensive literature review. We are unaware of anyone who has done this before, but I thought it might be worth leveraging the collective knowledge of folks on this list. Is anyone aware of any publications that describe such a study?

messages.body_plain:
Hi Quresh,

Not exactly citizen science, but we used data collected by managers over more than 40 years in an integrated population model with a Dail-Madsen model at its core, combined with a multistate capture-recapture model for survival and a Poisson regression for productivity.

Best regards,

José

Hi all. We are working on a data integration paper that combines professionally collected data with community science data to inform a Dail-Madsen style model (i.e., estimates population vital rates). Like everyone else, we want to claim our work is novel without necessarily implementing a rigorous and comprehensive literature review. We are unaware of anyone who has done this before, but I thought it might be worth leveraging the collective knowledge of folks on this list. Is anyone aware of any publications that describe such a study?

--
*** Three hierarchical modeling email lists ***
(1) unmarked: for questions specific to the R package unmarked
(2) SCR: for design and Bayesian or non-bayesian analysis of spatial capture-recapture
(3) HMecology (this list): for everything else, especially material covered in the books by Royle & Dorazio (2008), Kéry & Schaub (2012), Kéry & Royle (2016, 2021) and Schaub & Kéry (2022)
